newsitem.title: USA: Sears to spend $1.3 billion on stores.
newsitem.headline: Sears to spend $1.3 billion on stores.

text.p: Sears, Roebuck and Co chairman Arthur Martinez said Thursday the retailer planned to spend $1.3 billion this year on building new stores and upgrading existing outlets.
"One of our principal objectives is to grow," Martinez said at a breakfast meeting at which he announced the company's $1.3 billion capital spending plan and strong Christmas sales.
But Martinez issued some cautionary words about the outlook for the retail industry and the overall economy, which he forecast would grow more slowly in the second half of 1997.
He said that high levels of U.S. consumer debt needed to be "watched closely", but noted the rate of increase in credit card delinquencies had moderated after higher levels earlier in 1996.
"Credit card delinquencies have increased in 1996, but we have seen a moderation in that rate of increase in the last couple of months," Martinez said.
"It's to be watched closely, but we're not changing our credit strategies. We don't want to turn the spigot off and put a damper on our merchandise sales."
Looking ahead, Martinez said: "The momentum coming out of 1996 is very sustainable. We continue to look for market share gains in all of our businesses."
The retailer is committed to corporate growth.
"We have been public about our objective of generating mid- to high-teens earnings growth on a sustained basis and we are very confident about that projection for 1997," he said.
He declined to comment on a projection for 1996 year earnings of $1.36 a share. Martinez also noted that gross margins are favorable for December and the fourth quarter.
"We think we've reconnected with our customers," he added.

Martinez, who also serves on the board of the Chicago Federal Reserve Bank, said in his speech that he agreed with expectations of moderate U.S. economic growth in 1997 of between two percent and 2.5 percent, but warned that growth in the year's second half could slow.
He expressed concern about highly-leveraged consumers and said current law made it too easy to declare bankruptcy.
Earlier, Sears reported its comparable store sales for December rose 9.5 percent, while total sales increased 14.6 percent to $4.28 billion.

December's record sales reflected double-digit increases in women's, men's and children's apparel, shoes, accessories, cosmetics, fine jewelry and home fashions -- and in computers, electronics, tools and hardware.
